question.text: Find the determinant of the matrix $ N = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{6} & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & \sqrt{5} & 2\\ \sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
Notice that the $1$st row contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm{det}(N)&=\left| \begin{matrix} \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & \color{lightgray}0 & \color{lightgray}0 & \color{lightgray}0 \\ \color{lightgray}\sqrt{6} & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ \color{lightgray}5 & 0 & \sqrt{5} & 2 \\ \color{lightgray}\sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \end{matrix} \right|\\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot (-1 )^{1+1} \left|\begin{matrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \end{matrix}\right| \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot \left|\begin{matrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \end{matrix}\right| \end{align*}

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} 2 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-1} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{\sqrt{5}} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{\sqrt{5}} \end{vmatrix} &= 2 \cdot \left( (-1) \cdot \sqrt{5} \cdot \sqrt{5} \right) = -10. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain

\[ \det(N) = -10. \]

question.text: Find the determinant of the matrix $ B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 2 & 8 \\ 9 & 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
Notice that the $3$rd column contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

\begin{align} \det(B) &= \left|\begin{matrix} 5 & 0 & \color{lightgray}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & \color{lightgray}0 & 0 \\ \color{lightgray}-4 & \color{lightgray}1 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2}& \color{lightgray}8 \\ 9 & 0 & \color{lightgray}0 & -1 \end{matrix}\right| \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot (-1 )^{3+3} \left|\begin{matrix} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & 0 \\ 9& 0 & -1 \end{matrix}\right| \\[5pt] &= 2\cdot \left|\begin{matrix} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & 0 \\ 9& 0 & -1 \end{matrix}\right| \end{align}

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} 2\cdot \begin{vmatrix} \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{5} & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{6} & 0 \\ 9 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-1} \end{vmatrix} &= 2\cdot 5 \cdot 6 \cdot (-1) = -60. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain

\[ \det(B) = -60. \]

question.text:
Given that $\det(A^T)=7$, which of the following statements are true?

  1. $3\textrm{det}(A)=21$
  2. $-2\textrm{det}(A^T)=14$
  3. $\textrm{det}(A)+2\textrm{det}(I)=9$
question.explanation:
From the properties of determinants, we know that \[ \textrm{det}(A)=\textrm{det}(A^T) =7 \] and \[ \det(I) = 1. \]

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, \[ 3\textrm{det}(A)=3\cdot 7= 21. \]

  • Statement II is false. We have \[ -2\textrm{det}(A^T)=-2\cdot7=-14 \neq 14. \]

  • Statement III is true. We have \[ \textrm{det}(A)+2\textrm{det}(I)=7+2\cdot 1 = 9. \]

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and III only".

question.text:
Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

\[ \mathbf{a}= \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -7 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b}= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{c}= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -11 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ $\mathbf{c},$ and $\mathbf{d}{:}$

\[ M = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -7 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 4 & 0 \\ -2 & 8 & -11 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \]

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M{:}$

\[ V = | \det(M) | \]

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. So, we have

\[ \det(M) = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -7 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{4} & 0 \\ -2 & 8 & -11 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-2} \end{bmatrix} = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot (-2) = -72. \]

Therefore, the volume is

\[ V = | \det(M) | = |-72| = 72. \]

example.title: Computing the Volume of an N-Dimensional Parallelepiped

question.text:
Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

\[ \mathbf{a}= \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b}= \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \\ 4 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{c}= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}= \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 1 \\ 6 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ $\mathbf{c},$ and $\mathbf{d}{:}$

\[ M = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 5 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \]

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M{:}$

\[ V = | \det(M) | \]

Notice that the $3$rd column of the determinant contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

\begin{align*} \det(M) &= \left|\begin{matrix} -2 & 5 & \color{lightgray}0 & 7 \\ 0 & 4 & \color{lightgray}0 & 1 \\ \color{lightgray}1 & \color{lightgray}4 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt] 3 & \color{lightgray}6 \\ 0 & 0 & \color{lightgray}0 & 5 \end{matrix}\right| \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot (-1)^{3+3} \left|\begin{matrix} -2 & 5& 7 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{matrix}\right| \\[5pt] &= 3 \left|\begin{matrix} -2 & 5& 7 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{matrix}\right|. \end{align*}

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \det(M) &= 3 \begin{vmatrix} \bbox[lightgray, 2pt] {-2} & 5& 7 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt] 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt] 5 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot (-2) \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \\[5pt] &= -120 \end{align*}

Therefore, the volume is

\[ V = | \det(M) | = |-120| = 120. \]
